Stomacher
STUM-uh-ker
noun
From Middle English, an ornamental panel worn over chest and stomach; rendering Hebrew pethīgīl, a rich festal robe — the last article of Zion’s finery, exchanged in judgment for sackcloth.

Biblical Definition

The stomacher is the last garment named in the inventory, and it appears only in the sentence of exchange that closes it: “And it shall come to pass, that instead of sweet smell there shall be stink; and instead of a girdle a rent; and instead of well set hair baldness; and instead of a stomacher a girding of sackcloth; and burning instead of beauty” (Isa 3:24). Five exchanges, each a fashion undressed to its opposite: perfume to stench, sash to rope, coiffure to shaved scalp, festal robe to mourning cloth, beauty to branding. The stomacher was the showpiece — the rich panel worn over the breast, the glory-garment of a feast day — and the LORD trades it straight across for sackcloth, the fabric of grief. This is the inventory’s terrible arithmetic: everything the heart had banked in appearance converts, at judgment’s exchange-rate, into its own mockery. Yet Scripture does not leave the exchange running only one way. The same prophet announces the reversal for the penitent: “beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness” (Isa 61:3). The LORD who strips stomacher to sackcloth also clothes sackcloth with gladness: “thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness” (Psa 30:11). Let the believer choose which exchange he stands in — pride’s wardrobe converted downward, or mourning converted up, by grace, into the garments of salvation.

Webster 1828 Definition

The festal breast-robe closing Zion’s inventory, traded for sackcloth — judgment’s exchange-rate on appearance, and grace’s counter-exchange for the penitent.

STOMACHER, a rich ornamental panel or robe worn over the breast; Hebrew pethīgīl.

The last article of Zion’s finery, named only in the closing exchange (Isa 3:24).

Five trades: perfume to stink, girdle to rent, hair to baldness, stomacher to sackcloth, beauty to burning.

Everything banked in appearance converts, at judgment, into its own mockery.

Grace runs the exchange upward: beauty for ashes, gladness for sackcloth.

Key Scripture

Isa 3:24 — "And it shall come to pass, that instead of sweet smell there shall be stink; and instead of a girdle a rent; and instead of well set hair baldness; and instead of a stomacher a girding of sackcloth; and burning instead of beauty."

Isa 61:3 — "To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified."

Psa 30:11 — "Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness;"

1Pe 5:5 — "Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble."

Modern Corruption

Judgment’s exchange-rate on appearance: the showpiece robe converts to sackcloth — while grace runs the counter-exchange, beauty for ashes, for the penitent.

expand to see more

The corruption is banking the self in appearance. Zion’s daughters held their worth in fabric and fragrance, and Isaiah publishes the conversion table for that currency: stink for sweetness, sackcloth for the stomacher, burning instead of beauty. Every culture of image-worship carries the same fine print, and the present one most of all.

The recovered principle is the double exchange. The proud wardrobe converts downward at judgment; but the mourner’s sackcloth converts upward by grace — beauty for ashes, the garment of praise for heaviness, gladness girded on by God’s own hand. Be clothed with humility (1Pe 5:5): it is the one garment judgment cannot strip and the fabric grace loves to gild.

Hebrew Roots

Rendering the Hebrew pethigil, the stomacher is the festal showpiece traded for sackcloth in Isaiah’s closing exchange — and reversed for the penitent in Isaiah 61.
